passages.happening:
Chapter 6 ended with a question: when the great day comes, ‘who is able to withstand it?’ Before the seventh seal is opened, John is shown the answer.

“After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back its four winds so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree” (verse 1).

“And I saw another angel ascending from the east, with the seal of the living God” (verse 2). He calls out with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm the land and the sea: “Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have sealed the foreheads of the servants of our God” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is a pause between the sixth and seventh seals. The storm is held back, and nothing more happens until God has marked his own.

‘The four corners of the earth’ and ‘the four winds’ are a way of speaking about the whole world. Four is the number of the world in Revelation. The winds are the forces of harm, held in check by God's angels.

Then an angel comes with ‘the seal of the living God’. The Greek verb, sphragizō, means to mark with a seal as a sign of ownership and protection. In the first hearers' world, belonging was often shown in public. Slaves could be branded. Soldiers were sometimes marked with the sign of their unit. People devoted to certain gods bore their god's sign. To be sealed on the forehead was to belong to someone openly. For small churches under social and economic pressure, the picture told them that God had already marked them as his, whatever the empire might demand.

Paul uses the same verb for the Holy Spirit's seal on believers. And notice what the seal does not do. It does not keep God's people from all suffering. Later in this chapter they are seen ‘out of the great tribulation’. The seal promises that they belong to God through it.
passages.ot:
The sealing comes from Ezekiel's vision. Before judgment fell on Jerusalem, God told a man with a writing case to go through the city and “put a mark on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there” (Ezekiel 9:4). Those marked were spared.

Behind that stands the Passover, where the blood on the doorposts marked the houses that the destroyer would pass over: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13).

The four winds are Daniel's and Zechariah's. Daniel saw “the four winds of heaven were churning up the great sea” (Daniel 7:2), and Zechariah was told of “the four spirits of heaven, going forth from their station before the Lord of all the earth” (Zechariah 6:5).
passages.asks: Ask what it would mean for you to believe that God has marked you as his own. Ask whose mark you carry in public: in your work, your spending, your loyalties. And ask whether you expect belonging to God to keep you from all trouble, or to keep you through it.

passages.happening:
John does not see the sealed at first. He hears how many they are: “And I heard the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel” (verse 4).

Then he hears them counted, tribe by tribe, twelve thousand from each: Judah, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph and Benjamin (verses 5-8).
passages.hearers:
The number is built from twelve, the number of the tribes of Israel and of God's people. Twelve times twelve times a thousand is a figure of completeness. None of God's own is missing.

The list reads like a census of an army. In the book of Numbers, Israel's men were counted tribe by tribe for battle. Many readers think the list is meant to sound that way: God's people, numbered and ready.

The list is also unusual. Judah comes first, not Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob. That is most likely because the Messiah is ‘the Lion of the tribe of Judah’ (5:5). Dan is missing. Joseph is named where Ephraim might be expected. Levi, usually left out of lists of the tribes' land, is included. No one knows for certain why. Many note that Dan and Ephraim were linked with idol worship in Israel's history, but that is a suggestion, not something the text says.
passages.ot:
The counting is like Israel's census in the wilderness: “Take a census of the whole congregation of Israel by their clans and families” (Numbers 1:2), of “everyone who can serve in Israel’s army” (Numbers 1:3).

And twelve tribes, each named, go back to the twelve sons of Jacob in Genesis. God's people in Revelation are always tied to Israel's story.
passages.hard:
Who are the 144,000, and are they the same as the great multitude in the next verses?

Christians read this in several ways. Many futurists, especially dispensationalists, take the 144,000 as a group of Jewish believers sealed during a future time of trouble, distinct from the multitude of believers from the nations in verse 9. Others take them as Jewish Christians within the early church, set beside believers from the nations. A large number of interpreters across the traditions, Richard Bauckham among them, read the 144,000 and the multitude as the same people seen two ways: the whole church pictured first as the true Israel arranged like an army, then as the countless crowd from every nation. They point to the hear-then-see pattern of chapter 5, where John heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb, and to the way the New Testament calls those who belong to Christ ‘Abraham’s seed’ (Galatians 3:29). The 144,000 appear again in 14:1-5, which is part of the same discussion.

This is a question on which faithful readers differ, and these notes do not choose. Nothing in this passage speaks against the Jewish people, and no reading of it should be turned against them. These notes also make no claim that any church, group or movement of our own day is the 144,000.

The chapter's plain point stands on every reading. God knows his own by name and by number, and none of them is lost.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that God counts his people so carefully. Ask whether you think of yourself as part of a people with a long history, going back to Israel. And ask how you would answer someone who claimed that only their own group is the 144,000.

passages.t: A multitude no one could count
passages.happening:
John heard a number. Now he looks, and sees: “After this I looked and saw a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands” (verse 9).

He hears them cry out: “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (verse 10).

All the angels around the throne, the elders and the living creatures fall on their faces and worship God, saying: “Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanks and honor and power and strength be to our God forever and ever! Amen” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the great worship scenes of the book, and it answers chapter 6. Who can stand on the great day? This crowd is ‘standing before the throne and before the Lamb’.

The crowd is too large to count. It comes ‘from every nation and tribe and people and tongue’. In chapter 5 the Lamb's blood bought people from every nation. Here they are, gathered. God promised Abraham that his family would be beyond counting. This is that promise kept.

They wear white robes and hold palm branches. Palm branches were waved at the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived in shelters and rejoiced before God for seven days, and they were waved at celebrations of victory. This crowd is keeping a festival.

Their song is short: ‘Salvation to our God ... and to the Lamb’. Salvation is not their achievement. It belongs to God, and it comes through the Lamb. And again the one on the throne and the Lamb are praised together.

The angels answer with a sevenfold song, framed by ‘Amen’ at both ends: blessing, glory, wisdom, thanks, honour, power and strength. Seven is the number of completeness. Heaven holds nothing back.
passages.ot:
God's promise to Abraham is the root of this crowd: “Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able.” Then He told him, “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5).

And the palm branches are from the Feast of Tabernacles: “On the first day you are to gather the fruit of majestic trees, the branches of palm trees, and the boughs of leafy trees and of willows of the brook. And you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days” (Leviticus 23:40).
passages.asks: Ask how this picture of a crowd from every nation challenges the way you picture the church. Ask who you find it hardest to imagine standing beside you before the throne. And ask whether you can say, with this crowd, that your salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb, and not to you.

passages.t: Who are these in white robes?
passages.happening:
One of the elders asks John a question: “These in white robes,” he asked, “who are they, and where have they come from?” (verse 13). John hands the question back: “Sir,” I answered, “you know” (verse 14).

The elder explains: “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (verse 14). “For this reason, they are before the throne of God and serve Him day and night in His temple; and the One seated on the throne will spread His tabernacle over them” (verse 15).

“‘Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst; nor will the sun beat down upon them, nor any scorching heat.’ For the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd. ‘He will lead them to springs of living water,’ and ‘God will wipe away every tear from their eyes’” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
The elder asks a question he already knows the answer to, as an angel does with the prophet in Zechariah's visions. Then he explains.

These people have ‘come out of the great tribulation’. The Greek word thlipsis means pressure, being pressed or crushed. John already called himself a partner in the tribulation (1:9). These are people who went through it, not around it.

‘They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.’ It is a picture that cannot work in ordinary life: washing in blood makes cloth red, not white. That is the point. It is the Lamb's death, not their own record, that makes them clean.

‘The One seated on the throne will spread His tabernacle over them.’ The verb, skēnoō, means to pitch a tent. It recalls the tent where God lived among Israel in the wilderness, and the Feast of Tabernacles again. John's Gospel uses the same verb for the Word who became flesh and ‘made His dwelling among us’. God will live with them, and shelter them.

And the promises at the end are bodily and close. No more hunger. No more thirst. No more scorching heat. The hope is not escape from bodily life but its healing.

Then the most surprising line: ‘the Lamb ... will be their shepherd’. The Lamb becomes the shepherd. The one who died for the flock now guides it. Jesus called himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. Here that shepherd leads his people to living water, and God himself wipes the tears from their eyes.
passages.ot:
The last verses weave together two promises from Isaiah. “They will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them. For He who has compassion on them will guide them and lead them beside springs of water” (Isaiah 49:10). And “He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8).

‘The great tribulation’ recalls Daniel: “There will be a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time” (Daniel 12:1).

And the shepherd is the psalm's: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1).
passages.hard:
What is ‘the great tribulation’, and when is it?

The phrase recalls Daniel 12:1, and Jesus' words, “For at that time there will be great tribulation, unmatched from the beginning of the world until now” (Matthew 24:21). Christians read it in more than one way. Preterists connect it with the sufferings of the first century, including the Jewish war of AD 66 to 70 and the persecutions of Rome. Futurists read it as a final period of distress before Christ returns. Idealists and many others read it as the whole span of the church's suffering, which the New Testament treats as already under way: “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). These notes do not choose, and they set no date.

On every reading, these people did not escape trouble. They came through it, and the Lamb brought them out. The picture is not meant to frighten anyone. It is a promise to the suffering that their faithfulness is not wasted.
passages.asks: Ask what tears you are carrying that you most want God to wipe away. Ask what it means to you that the Lamb who died for you is also the shepherd who leads you. And ask whether you are trying to make your own robes white, or trusting the Lamb to do it.
